hook: Read a short literary scene closely: unpack participial clauses, sit with a paradox and turn images into plain meaning.
intro: An original short prose passage: a woman holds an unopened letter as evening falls, remembers a quarrel twenty years ago, finally reads it, and finds that it changes everything and nothing. The text works through delay (ohne ihn zu öffnen; irgendwann, als die Straßenlaternen angingen), paradox (nicht wiedererkannte und doch zu kennen glaubte), images that mirror her state (the roofs losing their colour and edges; the words falling like stones into water) and three participial clauses typical of literary German. It is told in the third person but stays close to her perceptions and thoughts (dachte sie). The questions ask about perspective, the effect of images, atmosphere and attitude — so translate each image into plain words before you choose.
tips[0].title: Participial clauses: literary compression
tips[0].text: A participle with its objects, set off by a comma, replaces a whole clause: Partizip I for something happening at the same time (haltend = while she held), Partizip II for a completed state or a passive (heraufgeweht = having been carried up; gezogen = with her knees drawn up). The subject is the subject of the main clause.
tips[0].check.why: He is in a completed state (worn out), so the clause takes Partizip II; Partizip I erschöpfend would mean 'exhausting' and describe the cause.
tips[0].visual.rows[0].a: Am Fenster stehend, sah sie den Regen.
tips[0].visual.rows[0].b: Während sie am Fenster stand, sah sie den Regen.
tips[1].title: Paradox and delay build tension
tips[1].text: The text withholds: she does not open the letter, the sender is never named, the content is never quoted. Paradoxes (known and unknown; everything and nothing; too late and just in time) name a state the woman cannot resolve. Effect questions want this tension named — not a fact the text never gives.
tips[1].trap: Do not fill the gaps: the text never says who wrote the letter or who moved out. Options that name the sender are "nicht im Text".
tips[1].check.why: Waiting and hoping she won't come is a paradox: it names a tension, and the text gives no fact about whether she comes.
tips[2].title: Translate the image, then answer
tips[2].text: Say the image in plain words first. Stones in water: heavy, they sink, the ripples keep widening → lasting, growing effect. Roofs losing colour and edges → certainties blurring. Furniture moved a few centimetres → the same room, yet different.
tips[2].check.why: Fog in the morning sun thins and disappears, so the image says her anger dissolved.
remember[0]: Participial clauses: haltend (at the same time), heraufgeweht / gezogen (state or passive) — the subject is that of the main clause.
remember[1]: Paradox, delay, images: name the effect in plain words; never fill in what the text withholds.
exam: Literary and essayistic passages appear in C1 exam reading — and reading perspective and images is what opens up a German novel.
tips[1].check.q: 'Er wartete auf sie und hoffte doch, sie würde nicht kommen.' What does this line create?
tips[1].check.options[0]: An inner conflict the text leaves open
tips[1].check.options[1]: A fact: she will not come
tips[1].check.options[2]: The reason why he is waiting
tips[1].check.answer: An inner conflict the text leaves open
tips[2].check.q: 'Ihre Wut verflog wie Nebel in der Morgensonne.' What does the image say in plain words?
tips[2].check.options[2]: She went out in the morning
